Juvenile Graytail skates (Bathyraja griseocauda) emerge from their egg cases at a relatively substantial size compared to many other skates, with a total length at birth measured at approximately 28 centimeters [Lb = approximately 28 centimeters]. This large neonatal size, representing roughly 18% of the body length ultimately attained by adults, is a trait shared among several congeners and likely serves to reduce vulnerability to gape-limited predators during the earliest demersal life stages. Early growth rates are influenced by the cool bottom temperatures characteristic of the species' deepwater habitat. Field observations from the southwestern Atlantic indicate that neonates begin foraging on small benthic crustaceans shortly after hatching, and their endogenous yolk reserves are typically fully depleted within the first several months. The extended incubation period and large size at birth are thought to reflect a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring survival over fecundity, a pattern observed across many deep-dwelling Bathyraja species that experience relatively stable but resource-poor environments.

The ultimate total length reached by Bathyraja griseocauda has been documented at 157 centimeters [Li = 157 centimeters], making it one of the larger members of the genus inhabiting the continental slope off southern South America. This maximum size is typically attained by females, who exhibit pronounced sexual dimorphism in overall dimensions compared to males. Corresponding to this considerable skeletal frame, the ultimate wet weight recorded for the species reaches approximately 36,600 grams [Wwi = approximately 36,600 grams], a figure derived from morphometric relationships established across the species' geographic range. This substantial body mass reflects the energetic demands of a slow-growing, long-lived predator that occupies a high trophic position within its benthic community. Deepwater trawl surveys have consistently captured mature individuals exceeding one meter in total length, confirming that the species regularly achieves its asymptotic dimensions under natural conditions, though growth rates decelerate markedly after the onset of reproductive maturity.

Puberty in Graytail skate is attained when individuals reach a total length of approximately 112 centimeters [Lp = approximately 112 centimeters], a size that corresponds to roughly 70% of the species' ultimate length. This developmental milestone marks the onset of gonadal activity and the potential for reproductive contribution to the population. Males typically mature at a slightly smaller mean size than females, a common pattern among elasmobranchs linked to differential energetic investment in gamete production and brooding. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from captured specimens reveals that testicular recrudescence and ovarian follicle development commence around this length threshold, with the first batches of mature oocytes appearing shortly thereafter. The attainment of sexual maturity at such a considerable body size suggests that Bathyraja griseocauda delays reproduction until a sufficiently large physical frame is achieved, a strategy that may enhance the survival prospects of both the parent and the offspring produced during the early reproductive years.

Estimated life-history parameters for Bathyraja griseocauda, derived from mark-recapture studies and demographic modeling, indicate that under typical thermal conditions found on the outer continental shelf at approximately 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the maximum lifespan reaches around 28 years [am = around 28 years]. This extended longevity is characteristic of many deepwater rajiforms, which exhibit slow metabolic rates and delayed senescence. Data from vertebral banding patterns suggest that the species experiences low natural mortality rates once past the juvenile stage, a demographic advantage in a relatively predator-scarce environment. Within this same thermal regime, the age at birth, encompassing the full embryonic development period within the egg case, has been estimated at approximately 730 days [ab = approximately 730 days] at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This remarkably protracted incubation is among the longest recorded for any skate species and underscores the profound influence of cold temperature on developmental pace in deep-sea ecosystems.

Reproductive output in Bathyraja griseocauda is characterized by a modest fecundity, with mature females producing a single egg case per oviposition event [N_R_i = single egg case per oviposition event] and depositing cases at a frequency of approximately 20 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 20 clutches per year] when held at ambient deepwater temperatures near 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This low rate of offspring production, combined with the extended two-year incubation period, results in a very slow potential rate of population increase. Each egg case, roughly 15 centimeters in length, contains a single developing embryo that relies entirely on its yolk reserve for the duration of incubation. The reproductive strategy thus emphasizes the production of well-provisioned, large-bodied neonates that are immediately capable of independent foraging and predator avoidance upon hatching. Such life-history traits render the species particularly vulnerable to overexploitation, as recovery from population depletion is expected to occur over decadal timescales given the protracted generation time and limited annual recruitment.
